summary:
Lua Navigator is a 3D web app that lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates in seconds. It shows the Sun and Earth relative to the horizon, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, a 30-day timeline, and a side-by-side site comparison. Built on astronomy-engine ephemerides and NASA LRO and LOLA data, it helps teams quickly find alternatives when a launch slips. Next step: real terrain horizons from LOLA.

This is a prototype. Our next step is deriving real terrain horizons from LOLA elevation data.
details:
What it does and how it works
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web app for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates. The user selects a site (or enters custom coordinates) and a date. The app computes where the Sun and Earth are relative to the local horizon, then shows: live Sun and Earth elevation, countdowns to sunset and Earthset, a 30-day elevation timeline with sunlight windows highlighted, solar coverage and Earth-visibility percentages, the longest shadow gap, and a side-by-side comparison matrix of candidate sites. A synchronized 3D Moon shows the sightlines to the Sun and Earth, colored by whether each is visible. Each site receives an explainable GO / CAUTION / NO-GO score that lists the factors behind it.

Benefits and intended impact
Today, evaluating a site-date pair means moving between several specialist tools. Our app puts the key answers (power and direct-to-Earth communication) in one view, so planners can quickly find alternatives when a launch slips, and so educators and the public can see why the Moon’s poles are so challenging for engineers.

Tools and technologies

  • JavaScript (ES modules), HTML/CSS, built with Vite
  • Three.js for the 3D Moon (vertex displacement from elevation data, orbit camera, dynamic Sun lighting)
  • HTML Canvas for the polar sky-dome radar, the timeline chart, and the model visualizer
  • astronomy-engine for Sun and Moon positions, combined with the IAU lunar orientation model (including libration) to compute azimuth and elevation from any lunar surface point
  • A JPL Horizons REST API client, plus deep links to LROC Quickmap and NASA Moon Trek
  • NASA data: LRO LROC imagery and LOLA topography (as 3D textures: color, hillshade, slope)

Creativity
We designed the app like a mission-control dashboard: a polar radar of the lunar sky with the terrain silhouette, a 3D Moon with live sightlines, site pins colored by score, and a time scrubber with scenario presets, all in one screen so that non-specialists can read it at a glance.
